Speaking about challenges…

5 min

They say nothing worth your while comes easy. Think about something you accomplished or created that was really hard to do.

  • How did you face that challenge?
  • How did you feel afterwards?

We respect your privacy, so don't share anything you don't want to!

Get in the mood for today by reflecting on what it took to face a big challenge. Building a StoryQuest is complex, so it helps to remember that practice makes progress. To be honest, we don't expect anything to be perfect here - this is a learning experience where you're supposed to have fun. It's not a race!

The Teleporter Challenge

25 min

This is the Teleporter Challenge - an exercise to keep practicing with Godot. This is not your StoryQuest yet. You'll take a working teleporter from a scene in the StoryQuest Kit, get it functioning in a scene of your own, and make it your own.

  • Start by exploring how the teleporter works in an existing scene.
  • Then move the teleporter into a new scene, and customize it.

Tip: from now on, whenever you make a change in your Godot project, play it. See how it feels.

What might your teleporter look like?

Now you have a mechanic set! But a teleporter you can't see when you play feels… off. Time to make it visible - and to give it a bit of story.

Right now, the teleporter is just a space that moves the player from A to B, so visually it could become almost anything. What could you make it look like, and what might that tell a player about the world around it? That's a small piece of game narrative.

Let's quickly brainstorm what this teleporter might be. You can imagine some story around it first, or just start describing the object itself and see what ideas emerge. The more specific you get, the more you'll have to work with when you draw it.

Some context for the object

  • What's it for, and who uses it?
  • Did characters in your quest make it for a purpose, or was it always there and they've discovered it?
  • Is it an everyday thing, or is something strange going on and the object looks out of place?
  • Is it welcoming, or does it feel a bit dangerous? Would you walk straight up to it, or stand there warily first?
  • What's it going to feel like to use it - sudden and fast, or slow and calm? Are you moving, or is reality moving around you?

Describing the object itself

More detail offers clues. Start plain, then keep adding - watch how a story appears:

  • It's a door.
  • → An old wooden door, hanging slightly off its hinges.
  • → It's the door of a cabin nobody has been to in years.
  • → The planks don't line up any more - there are gaps you can see through.
  • → One part looks deliberately damaged.

You don't need a whole story, just a sentence or two. This stays on your device - jot it here, then draw it in the guide.

Share

No two are alike

5 min

Share what you made:

  • Take a screenshot of your newly drawn teleporter in your scene.
  • Share the screenshot with someone, and ask what they think it suggests about the place, story, or world around it.
  • Afterwards, tell them what you were hoping the teleporter would communicate.

Your task

  • 1Post in the Feed: share your teleporter scene - a screenshot, or a playable link - and don't forget to mention the narrative concept behind it.

Want to share a playable link to your scene? The Sharing with Backstitch guide shows you how - it's a really cool feature you'll use again later in the program.
